title: Ecology
description: How organisms live together: ecosystems, food chains, nutrient cycles, relationships and human impact.
objectives: Construct food chains and explain energy loss

topics.title: Ecosystems and Feeding
topics.description: Habitats, populations and communities; food chains, webs and pyramids.

lessons.title: Habitats and Populations
lessons.description: The ecological address system: habitat, population, community, ecosystem, biome.
objectives: Define habitat, population, community, ecosystem and niche
Distinguish biotic from abiotic factors with examples
Explain how one abiotic factor limits a named population
lessons.introduction: A tilapia's world is water temperature, dissolved oxygen, algae to eat and fishermen to avoid. Ecology maps these worlds — and what happens when they change.

contents.title: The address system
contents.body: HABITAT: where an organism lives (a fishpond, a mango canopy). POPULATION: all members of ONE species in a habitat (all tilapia in the pond). COMMUNITY: ALL populations sharing the habitat (tilapia + catfish + algae + water insects). ECOSYSTEM: community PLUS non-living surroundings (water, mud, sunlight, dissolved oxygen). BIOME: a continental-scale ecosystem type (tropical rainforest, savanna, desert). NICHE: an organism's ROLE — what it eats, what eats it, when it is active (no two species hold identical niches for long — competition excludes one). Factors splitting the world: BIOTIC (living: predation, competition, disease, food supply) and ABIOTIC (non-living: light, temperature, water, pH, salinity, oxygen). Examination habit: always classify factors before explaining effects.

contents.title: Worked example: why did the fish die?
contents.body: Question: After hot harmattan weeks, fish die in a shallow pond though no poison is found. Explain using abiotic factors. Step 1 — Identify the factor: high temperature LOWERS dissolved oxygen in water (warm water holds less gas) while fish metabolism (oxygen demand) RISES. Step 2 — Link: demand exceeds supply, especially at night when algae also respire. Step 3 — Conclude: fish suffocate — an abiotic (temperature/oxygen) population crash with no disease needed. Management moral: shade, aeration or deeper ponds buffer the factor. Examiners award the gas-solubility link specifically — memorise it.

contents.title: Key concepts
contents.body:
Habitat (address) → population (one species) → community (all species) → ecosystem (+ non-living) → biome (continental).
Niche = role; competitive exclusion forbids identical niches.
Biotic = living pressures; abiotic = physical/chemical conditions.
Warm water holds less oxygen while raising demand — classic fish-kill mechanism.

contents.title: Lesson summary
contents.body: Ecology's vocabulary maps where organisms live and what constrains them. Populations answer to both living neighbours and non-living conditions — and a single abiotic shift can crash a pond.

references: OpenStax Biology 2e — Chapter 42, Ecosystems (levels of ecology)

lessons.title: Food Chains and Energy Flow
lessons.description: Producers to top predators: why energy pyramids narrow and chains stay short.
objectives: Construct food chains with correct trophic levels and arrows
Interpret pyramids of number, biomass and energy
lessons.introduction: It takes roughly 10 kg of grain to make 1 kg of beef. Follow the energy and you will understand farming, famine and why there are no six-metre spiders.

contents.title: Trophic levels
contents.body: PRODUCERS (autotrophs — grass, algae) capture sunlight. PRIMARY CONSUMERS (herbivores — grasshopper, tilapia fry) eat producers. SECONDARY CONSUMERS (small carnivores — frog, catfish) eat herbivores. TERTIARY CONSUMERS (top predators — hawk, crocodile) eat carnivores. DECOMPOSERS (bacteria, fungi) digest dead matter and waste at EVERY level, recycling nutrients. Arrows point IN THE DIRECTION OF ENERGY FLOW (food → feeder): grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → hawk. Real feeding is a WEB (owls eat both mice and frogs), but chains isolate one path for analysis. TROPHIC LEVEL = feeding step counted from producers (level 1).

contents.title: Why pyramids narrow
contents.body: Only ~10% of energy transfers between levels: most is lost to RESPIRATION (movement, warmth, metabolism), UNEATEN parts (roots, bones), INEDIBLE parts (bark, fur) and EXCRETION (urine, faeces, egested fibre). Consequences: (1) food chains rarely exceed 4–5 levels — too little energy remains; (2) top predators are few (one lion needs thousands of kg of grass via zebras); (3) eating lower (grains, beans) feeds more people per hectare than beef — a food-security arithmetic every policymaker should know. PYRAMIDS: energy pyramids ALWAYS narrow upward; biomass pyramids usually narrow (but can invert — e.g. tiny fast-reproducing phytoplankton supporting heavier zooplankton); number pyramids can invert (one tree feeding thousands of insects). Biomagnification runs opposite: persistent toxins (mercury, some pesticides) CONCENTRATE upward, poisoning top predators most.

contents.title: Worked example: the missing energy
contents.body: Question: A grassland fixes 20,000 kJ/m²/year. Zebras gain 1,800 kJ; lions gain 160 kJ. Calculate both transfer efficiencies and account for the losses. Step 1 — Efficiencies: zebra 1800/20000 = 9%; lion 160/1800 ≈ 9%. Step 2 — Losses: grass respiration + uneaten roots + zebra respiration/movement/dung + lion respiration/movement/indigestible parts. Step 3 — Conclude: ~9% matches the 10% rule; each level keeps roughly one-tenth. Examination format: show the division, convert to %, then name at least THREE loss routes — respiration is compulsory in the list.

contents.title: Key concepts
contents.body:
Arrows show ENERGY flow: food → feeder. Decomposers recycle at every level.
~10% transfers; the rest respires, uneaten, indigestible or excreted.
Chains stay short; top predators stay few; low eating feeds more.
Toxins biomagnify upward — opposite to energy.

contents.title: Lesson summary
contents.body: Energy enters through producers and leaks ~90% at every step, shaping short chains, rare predators and the arithmetic of feeding humanity. Toxins, perversely, concentrate where energy fades.

references: OpenStax Biology 2e — Chapter 42 (energy flow, trophic levels)

topics.title: Cycles and Relationships
topics.description: Carbon and nitrogen cycles; predation, competition and symbiosis.

lessons.title: Carbon and Nitrogen Cycles
lessons.description: How the same atoms circulate through air, life and soil forever.
objectives: Trace carbon through photosynthesis, respiration, feeding and combustion
Explain nitrogen fixation, nitrification, denitrification and the role of bacteria
lessons.introduction: The carbon in your body was once dinosaur breath, ancient forest and ocean limestone. Atoms recycle endlessly — today's cycles are tomorrow's dinner.

contents.title: The carbon cycle
contents.body: Atmospheric CO2 enters life through PHOTOSYNTHESIS (producers). Carbon then moves through FEEDING (herbivores → carnivores), returns to air via RESPIRATION (all living cells), DECOMPOSITION (decomposers respiring dead matter), and COMBUSTION (burning wood, fossil fuels, bush fires). Oceans exchange CO2 at the surface; long-term stores (limestone, fossil fuels, peat) lock carbon for millennia. Humans unbalance the cycle by burning fossil stores millions of times faster than they formed — raising CO2, trapping heat (greenhouse effect) and acidifying oceans. Planting trees and protecting forests re-lock carbon; burning bush and flaring gas accelerate the imbalance.

contents.title: The nitrogen cycle
contents.body: Nitrogen gas (78% of air) is unusable directly — the triple bond defeats most life. Bacteria run the cycle: (1) NITROGEN FIXATION — Rhizobium in legume root nodules (beans, soya, groundnuts) and free-living Azotobacter convert N2 to ammonia; lightning fixes some too. (2) NITRIFICATION — Nitrosomonas convert ammonia → nitrites, then Nitrobacter convert nitrites → NITRATES, which plants absorb. (3) ASSIMILATION — plants build nitrates into amino acids and proteins; animals gain nitrogen by eating plants. (4) AMMONIFICATION/DECOMPOSITION — decomposers return nitrogen from dead matter, urine and faeces as ammonia. (5) DENITRIFICATION — anaerobic Pseudomonas convert nitrates BACK to N2 gas in waterlogged soils (a fertility loss farmers dread). Crop rotation with beans exploits fixation free of charge — traditional wisdom validated by microbiology.

contents.title: Worked example: the green, stinking lake
contents.body: Question: Fertiliser runoff enters a lake. Within weeks the water turns green, smells, and fish die. Explain (eutrophication). Step 1 — Nitrates/phosphates fertilise ALGAE → algal bloom (green water) blocking light; submerged plants die. Step 2 — Dead algae and plants feed DECOMPOSER bacteria, which multiply and RESPIRE heavily. Step 3 — Bacterial respiration strips dissolved OXYGEN (especially at night) → fish suffocate; anaerobic decay releases stinking gases (hydrogen sulphide). Step 4 — Conclude: nutrient enrichment → bloom → decomposition → deoxygenation → death. Prevention: buffer strips, precise fertiliser dosing, and treating sewage before discharge.

contents.title: Watch: Carbon and Nitrogen Cycles
contents.body: Watch 'Carbon and Nitrogen Cycles' by the Amoeba Sisters (official channel stream). Draw both cycles from memory afterwards, naming the bacteria in the nitrogen cycle.

contents.title: Key concepts
contents.body:
Carbon: photosynthesis in; respiration, decomposition, combustion out.
Nitrogen: fixation (Rhizobium) → nitrification (Nitrosomonas/Nitrobacter) → assimilation → decomposition → denitrification.
Legumes fertilise for free via root-nodule bacteria.
Eutrophication: nutrients → bloom → decay → deoxygenation → fish kill.

contents.title: Lesson summary
contents.body: Carbon cycles through air and life in years; nitrogen cycles through bacterial middlemen in soils. Both cycles feed us — and both punish careless fertiliser and fuel use.

lessons.title: How Species Relate
lessons.description: Predation, competition and the three symbioses — mutualism, commensalism, parasitism.
objectives: Define predation, competition and the three symbioses
Give two Nigerian examples of each relationship
lessons.introduction: Oxpeckers ride cattle eating ticks; mistletoe strangles orange trees; lions and leopards hunt the same antelope. Every ecosystem is a web of deals, thefts and wars.

contents.title: Five relationships
contents.body: PREDATION (+/−): hunter kills prey (lion/antelope, praying mantis/housefly) — drives cycles and natural selection. COMPETITION (−/−): both sides lose fitness fighting for the same resource — intraspecific (two yam seedlings crowding) is fiercest since needs match exactly; interspecific (goats vs cattle on grass) can exclude one species. MUTUALISM (+/+): both benefit — Rhizobium fixes nitrogen for beans while beans feed it sugars; oxpeckers clean cattle of ticks; gut bacteria digest fibre for us. COMMENSALISM (+/0): one benefits, the other unaffected — epiphytic ferns perch on trees for light; cattle egrets eat insects flushed by grazing herds. PARASITISM (+/−): parasite benefits, host suffers — Plasmodium (malaria), tapeworms, ticks, mistletoe on citrus. Grade relationships by FITNESS EFFECTS (+/−), not feelings.

contents.title: Predator-prey cycles
contents.body: Predator and prey populations oscillate in linked waves: many prey → predators feast and breed → many predators over-eat prey → prey crash → predators starve → few predators let prey recover — the cycle repeats with predators LAGGING behind prey (classic lynx-hare graphs). Human interference (pesticides killing predators, overfishing prey) breaks cycles and triggers plagues or collapses. Biological control EXPLOITS predation deliberately: ladybirds vs aphids, Bacillus thuringiensis vs mosquito larvae — pest control with minimal chemicals when done scientifically.

contents.title: Worked example: classifying relationships
contents.body: Question: Classify: (a) tapeworm in a child's gut, (b) egret following cattle, (c) lichen (fungus + alga). Step 1 — Score fitness effects: (a) worm gains food/shelter, child loses nutrients → (+/−) PARASITISM. (b) Egret gains flushed insects; cattle unaffected → (+/0) COMMENSALISM. (c) Fungus shelters algae; algae photosynthesise sugars for both → (+/+) MUTUALISM. Step 2 — Justify each with the benefit/harm mechanism. Examination trap: mutualism needs PROVEN two-way benefit — 'living together' alone is just symbiosis in the broad sense.

contents.title: Watch: Ecological Relationships
contents.body: Watch 'Ecological Relationships' by the Amoeba Sisters (official channel stream). Afterwards, classify five relationships you have personally observed at home or in the market.

contents.title: Key concepts
contents.body:
Predation +/−, competition −/−, mutualism +/+, commensalism +/0, parasitism +/−.
Intraspecific competition is fiercest (identical needs).
Predator peaks lag prey peaks in population cycles.
Biological control weaponises predation against pests.

contents.title: Lesson summary
contents.body: Species deal in five currencies from mutual profit to outright theft. Predator-prey cycles breathe through ecosystems, and wise farmers and doctors turn these relationships into tools.

topics.title: Humans and the Environment
topics.description: Pollution, habitat loss and climate change — and what conservation can do.

lessons.title: Impact and Conservation
lessons.description: Deforestation, pollution, overharvesting and climate change — causes, effects and solutions.
objectives: Explain four human impacts with mechanisms and effects
Propose three realistic local conservation actions
lessons.introduction: Nigeria loses hundreds of thousands of hectares of forest yearly; Lagos traffic chokes the air; the Sahel creeps south. Ecology without action is just watching — this lesson demands solutions.

contents.title: Four impacts
contents.body: (1) DEFORESTATION: logging, farming and fuelwood remove forests → biodiversity loss, soil erosion (no roots to hold soil), flooding, and CO2 release (fewer absorbers + burning). (2) POLLUTION: oil spills smother mangroves and fisheries (Niger Delta); plastic chokes drains and livestock; industrial effluent poisons rivers; vehicle exhaust harms lungs. (3) OVERHARVESTING: taking faster than replacement — overfishing collapses stocks (smaller catches yearly), bushmeat hunting empties forests ('empty forest syndrome'). (4) CLIMATE CHANGE: fossil-fuel CO2 traps heat → rising temperatures, erratic rainfall, sea-level rise threatening Lagos and the Delta, and shifting disease zones (malaria climbing to highlands). Each impact hits the poorest first — environmental damage is a justice issue.

contents.title: Conservation that works
contents.body: PRESERVATION locks nature away untouched; CONSERVATION manages use sustainably (harvest below replacement rate). Working tools: PROTECTED AREAS (Yankari, Cross River parks) guard biodiversity cores; REFORESTATION and agroforestry rebuild cover and income; SUSTAINABLE FISHING (size limits, closed seasons, no dynamite) lets stocks recover; WASTE MANAGEMENT (reduce, reuse, recycle; proper dumps, not drains); CLEAN ENERGY (solar leapfrogs grids); and EDUCATION — the multiplier of all the rest. Conservation succeeds when locals benefit: ecotourism jobs, beekeeping buffers, community forests. Your assignment investigates one local issue and proposes exactly such a plan.

contents.title: Worked example: the disappearing forest
contents.body: Question: A village clears riverside forest for yam mounds. Two years later: yam yields fall, the stream floods yearly, and fish vanish. Explain and propose fixes. Step 1 — Diagnose: no tree roots → soil ERODES into the stream (silt smothers fish eggs); no canopy → rain hits soil directly (flooding); no leaf litter → soil fertility CRASHES (yields fall). Step 2 — Prescribe: replant riverbank buffer trees (roots + shade), practise alley cropping (yam between nitrogen-fixing hedges), and ban farming within 10 m of the stream. Step 3 — Generalise: every symptom traces to removing the forest's free services — conservation is enlightened self-interest.

contents.title: Key concepts
contents.body:
Deforestation → erosion + floods + CO2. Pollution → dead zones + disease. Overharvesting → collapse. Climate change → heat + erratic rain + rising seas.
Conservation = sustainable use; preservation = no use.
Solutions must pay locals: ecotourism, agroforestry, closed seasons.
Forest services (soil, water, climate) are free until destroyed.

contents.title: Lesson summary
contents.body: Human impacts share one root: consuming natural capital faster than it renews. Conservation — protected areas, sustainable harvests, clean energy, educated citizens — is how civilisation pays its ecological bills.

practical.title: Compound Biodiversity Audit
practical.objective: Estimate plant populations with quadrats and compare biodiversity between two areas.
practical.scenario: You are an ecologist comparing a trampled path edge with an undisturbed corner.
practical.instructions: 1. Make a quadrat: 4 sticks + string forming a 50 cm × 50 cm square. 2. Throw it RANDOMLY (over your shoulder, no choosing) 5 times in AREA A (disturbed: path/football edge) and 5 times in AREA B (undisturbed: garden corner/bush edge). 3. In each throw, count every plant species (grass, weed types — name or sketch) and individuals per species. 4. Record: throw | species | counts. Calculate mean plants per quadrat and species count per area. 5. Conclude: which area is more diverse/abundant, and link to trampling, light or soil (abiotic factors). SAFETY: watch for thorns, ants and broken glass; wear closed shoes; wash hands.
practical.expected_output: Two 5-throw data tables with means + conclusion naming the likely causal factors.
evaluation_criteria: Conclusion links differences to specific biotic/abiotic factors

assignment.title: My Environment, My Plan
assignment.description: Investigate one real local environmental problem and write a costed, realistic action plan.
assignment.instructions: 1. Choose ONE issue near you: blocked drains, refuse dumps, tree loss, stream pollution, erosion, smoke, or overfishing. 2. EVIDENCE: describe what you observe (photos described, locations, who is affected, since when) — 150 words. 3. ECOLOGY: explain the biological mechanism (eutrophication? erosion? biomagnification? habitat loss?) — 150 words. 4. PLAN: propose 3 actions with WHO does WHAT, rough COST (free/cheap/expensive), and how success is MEASURED — 200 words. 5. Submit 500–600 words total. Real places and real numbers score highest.
assignment.requirements: Must be a real place you have visited; invented issues score zero.
evaluation_criteria: Concrete local evidence (place, observations, affected people)
Three realistic actions with owners, costs and success measures

quiz.title: Module 7 Quiz — Ecology
quiz.description: Quick check on ecosystems, energy flow, cycles and relationships.

questions.question: In a food chain, arrows point:
questions.explanation: Arrows follow ENERGY: grass → grasshopper means energy flows from grass into the grasshopper. (Predator-to-prey points backwards.)

questions.question: Only ~10% of energy transfers between trophic levels mainly because energy is lost through:
options: Respiration, movement, uneaten and indigestible parts, excretion
questions.explanation: Respiration burns most energy; plus uneaten roots/bones, indigestible fibre and excreted waste never become the next level's food.

questions.question: Rhizobium bacteria in bean root nodules perform:
questions.explanation: Rhizobium FIX nitrogen gas into ammonia for the plant (mutualism). Nitrosomonas/Nitrobacter nitrify; Pseudomonas denitrify.

questions.question: Oxpeckers eating ticks off cattle is:
questions.explanation: Both benefit: birds get food, cattle lose parasites (+/+). One-sided benefit would be commensalism; harm would be parasitism.

questions.question: Fish die after fertiliser runoff causes an algal bloom because:
options: Decomposer bacteria multiply on dead algae and strip dissolved oxygen
questions.explanation: Eutrophication: bloom → die-off → bacterial decomposition → deoxygenation → suffocation. The killer is oxygen loss, not the algae directly.

assessment.title: Module 7 Examination — Ecology
assessment.description: End-of-module examination covering ecosystems, cycles, relationships and conservation.
assessment.instructions: Answer ALL 6 questions in 25 minutes. Pass mark is 60%. Counts toward your final assessment gate.

questions.question: A hawk accumulates more pesticide than the grasshoppers it eats because of:
questions.explanation: Persistent toxins concentrate at each level, so top predators carry the highest load — the reverse pattern to energy flow.

questions.question: Which process RETURNS carbon dioxide to the atmosphere? (best single answer)
questions.explanation: All living respiration, decomposer decay and burning release CO2. Photosynthesis removes it; fixation concerns nitrogen.

questions.question: Waterlogged soils lose fertility partly because denitrifying bacteria:
options: Convert nitrates back to nitrogen gas in anaerobic conditions
questions.explanation: Without oxygen, denitrifiers (Pseudomonas) use nitrates for respiration, releasing N2 gas — nitrogen escapes back to the air.

questions.question: True or False: In predator-prey cycles, the predator population peak lags behind the prey peak.
questions.explanation: True. Prey must first become abundant to feed predator breeding; predators then over-eat prey and crash after them.

questions.question: Conservation differs from preservation in that conservation:
options: Bans all human use of nature
Manages sustainable use below replacement rates
questions.explanation: Conservation = wise sustainable use (fishing quotas, selective logging); preservation = locking away untouched.

questions.question: Which are abiotic factors? (Select ALL that apply)
questions.explanation: Light, pH and water are non-living (abiotic). Predation is a living (biotic) pressure.
